content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Column Statistics, Histograms, and Density in SQL Tuning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO) relies heavily on accurate database statistics to generate optimal execution plans. Among these, column statistics, histograms, and density metrics are the foundational elements used to estimate cardinality, which is the expected number of rows returned by an operation."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Role of Column Statistics"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Basic column statistics provide a high-level summary of the data distribution within a specific table column. These metrics are typically gathered by database statistics collection jobs (such as DBMS_STATS in Oracle or ANALYZE in PostgreSQL)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NUM_DISTINCT: The number of unique values in the column."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NUM_NULLS: The total number of null rows in the column."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE: The lower and upper bounds of the data."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Column Density"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Density is a metric representing the probability of finding a specific value in a column, assuming a uniform distribution (where applicable). It is typically calculated as the inverse of the number of distinct values (1 / NUM_DISTINCT). The CBO uses density to estimate selectivity when equality predicates involve bind variables or non-existent values."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"SELECT column_name, num_distinct, density, num_nulls FROM user_tab_cols WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS';"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"When Column Statistics Fall Short: Histograms"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Standard column statistics assume a uniform distribution of data. However, real-world data is frequently skewed, meaning certain values appear much more frequently than others. When data skew occurs, the uniformity assumption leads to poor cardinality estimates and suboptimal execution plans."},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Histograms solve this problem by describing the actual frequency and distribution of data values within specific ranges or buckets."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Frequency Histograms: Created when the number of distinct values is small and equals the number of buckets. Each distinct value gets its own bucket."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Height-Balanced Histograms: Used when the number of distinct values is large. Rows are divided into buckets so that each bucket contains approximately the same number of rows."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Gathering Custom Statistics with Histograms"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"DBAs can explicitly instruct the statistics gathering engine to build histograms on skewed columns where predicates are frequently applied."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS(ownname => 'SCHEMA', tabname => 'ORDERS', method_opt => 'for all columns size skewonly');"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Tuning Impact and Best Practices"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Stale or missing histograms are a primary root cause of sudden SQL performance degradation. If a query suddenly switches from an Index Range Scan to a Full Table Scan (or vice versa), verifying the presence and accuracy of histograms on the filtered columns should be an immediate troubleshooting step."}]
